summary: Describes using HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 in IPsec. These can provide data origin authentication and integrity checks for AH, ESP, IKE, and IKEv2, and can serve as pseudo-random functions. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC tells IPsec implementations how to use the SHA-2 hash functions, which produce 256, 384 or 512 bits of output, together with HMAC, the construction that mixes a secret key into a hash. The result is used in two ways: to tag packets so the receiver can tell they were not altered, and to generate the keys IPsec itself runs on.

questions: how to use hmac-sha-256 with ipsec
which hash algorithms does ipsec support
why is hmac output truncated in ipsec
what key length does hmac-sha-256 use in ipsec
subtitle: Using the SHA-2 hash family to authenticate and protect IPsec traffic.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs a way to prove that a packet came from the party it claims to come from and was not altered on the way, and it needs a way to generate the keys it uses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies HMAC built on SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, in two forms: truncated authenticators of 128, 192 and 256 bits for checking packets, and untruncated pseudo-random functions for generating keying material in IKE and IKEv2.
tldr.outcome: An IPsec implementation can use the SHA-2 family for both jobs, with fixed key lengths and truncations chosen so that a forged packet is as hard to produce as the birthday bound allows.

facts.label: Authenticator key length
facts.value: Equal to the hash output length

today: RFC 4868 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the algorithms it defines are still the ones it describes.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content:
The document specifies the use of SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 combined with HMAC as data origin authentication and integrity verification mechanisms for the IPsec Authentication Header, the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload, IKE and IKEv2. Output truncation is specified for these variants, and the truncated algorithms are named HMAC-SHA-256-128, HMAC-SHA-384-192 and HMAC-SHA-512-256. The truncation lengths follow the birthday bound of each algorithm.

The document also describes untruncated variants of the same algorithms used as pseudo-random functions for IKE and IKEv2, named PRF-HMAC-SHA-256, PRF-HMAC-SHA-384 and PRF-HMAC-SHA-512. The PRF algorithms and the authentication variants are called the HMAC-SHA-256+ algorithms throughout, where the plus sign means the family of algorithms built on SHA-256 and the larger hashes.

The two uses have different aims. The PRF variants provide secure pseudo-random functions for generating keying material and other protocol-specific numbers, while the authentication variants make sure that packets are authentic and cannot be modified in transit. In both cases the security depends on how the secret key is distributed and how unpredictable it is. If the key is unpredictable and known only to the sender and the recipient, then only parties holding the same key can derive the values that go with it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC covers two uses of the same hash functions. One produces a short tag that travels with a packet, so the receiver can check that nothing changed it. The other produces a long stream of unpredictable bits, used to make the keys that IPsec runs on. Both are only as safe as the key they use.

sections.title: The Keys
sections.content:
Three sizes matter and the document defines them precisely. The block size is the size of the data block the underlying hash works on, which is 512 bits for SHA-256 and 1024 bits for SHA-384 and SHA-512. The output length is the size of the hash value, which is 256 bits for SHA-256, 384 bits for SHA-384 and 512 bits for SHA-512. The authenticator length is the size of the authenticator in bits after truncation, and in this specification it is always half the output length of the hash.

For the authentication and integrity use, the key length is fixed. HMAC itself does not fix a key length, but this specification requires that a key length equal to the output length of the hash must be supported and that no other key length may be supported, so 256 bits for HMAC-SHA-256, 384 for SHA-384 and 512 for SHA-512. The reason is in part the advice in the HMAC document itself, that keys shorter than the output length reduce the strength while longer keys do not add much, and in part that variable key lengths would make IPsec implementations disagree with each other.

For the PRF use, key lengths may vary, and the rules for handling a key of any length follow the HMAC document. A key whose length is exactly the block size is used as it is. A shorter key is lengthened to the block size by padding it on the right with zero bits, which the document notes is a case HMAC discourages but which is described here because pre-shared keys for IKE and IKEv2 are often shorter. A key longer than the block size is shortened by computing the hash of the whole key and using that result as the key, which then needs the zero padding described above.

The key itself must come from a strong pseudo-random function, and no weak keys for these algorithms were known when the document was written. The key distribution mechanism has to make sure that unique keys are allocated and handed only to the parties taking part in the communication. The document also recommends refreshing keys periodically, as the HMAC document does, because it limits the damage of a key that is exposed. It notes that a brute force attack on a 256, 384 or 512-bit key would take longer than the universe has existed, while a weak key such as a dictionary word would be far easier to guess, so the lifetime chosen for a key has to take that into account.
sections.plainLanguage: When the hash checks a packet, the key must be exactly as long as the hash output: 256, 384 or 512 bits. When the hash generates keys, the key may be any length, and it is padded or hashed to fit. The key itself has to be random, and it has to be replaced from time to time so that a leak does not do lasting harm.

sections.title: Padding and Truncation
sections.content:
HMAC with SHA-256 works on 512-bit blocks, and HMAC with SHA-384 or SHA-512 works on 1024-bit blocks. The padding rules are those of the SHA-2 standard itself, so an implementation that follows that standard needs to add nothing further for these algorithms. As far as the implicit packet padding defined for the Authentication Header is concerned, no implicit packet padding is required.

Each algorithm produces a value whose length is the output length of the hash, for example 256 bits for HMAC-SHA-256. For use as an authenticator, that value may be truncated. When the algorithm is used as a data origin authentication and integrity verification mechanism in ESP, AH, IKE or IKEv2, a truncated value using the first nnn/2 bits, exactly half the algorithm output, must be supported, and no other authenticator lengths are supported by this specification.

The sending side stores the truncated value in the authenticator field. The receiving side computes the whole nnn-bit value and compares the first nnn/2 bits with what was stored. The length of half the output was chosen because it corresponds to the birthday attack bound of each algorithm, and at the same time it keeps the number of extra bits on the wire small.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag that travels with a packet is half the size of the hash output: 128 bits for SHA-256, 192 for SHA-384 and 256 for SHA-512. The sender puts the first half of the hash in the packet, and the receiver computes the full hash and compares the same half. Half is as much as the birthday bound allows.

sections.title: The Two Forms and Their Parameters
sections.content:
PRF-HMAC-SHA-256 is the same algorithm as HMAC-SHA-256-128 except that variable-length keys are permitted and the truncation step is not performed. PRF-HMAC-SHA-384 and PRF-HMAC-SHA-512 are the same as HMAC-SHA-384-192 and HMAC-SHA-512-256 in the same way: variable-length keys are permitted and no truncation is done. So the difference between the two families is only the key length rule and whether the output is cut in half.

The document also states that as of writing there are no known issues that prevent the HMAC-SHA-256+ algorithms from being used with any specific cipher algorithm.

The parameter summary in Section 2.6 gives, for each of the six algorithms, the block size, the output length, the truncation length, the key length and the algorithm type, where var stands for variable. For HMAC-SHA-256-128 the block size is 512, the output 256, the truncation 128 and the key 256, and the type is authentication and integrity. HMAC-SHA-384-192 has block size 1024, output 384, truncation 192 and key 384, and HMAC-SHA-512-256 has block size 1024, output 512, truncation 256 and key 512. The three PRF variants have the same block sizes and output lengths, no truncation, and a variable key length.
sections.plainLanguage: The same hash is used in two ways. As an authenticator the key must have a fixed length and the output is cut in half. As a pseudo-random function the key may be any length and the output is used whole. Beyond that the two forms behave identically.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The document gives test cases for each algorithm, each with a key, some data and the resulting authenticator or PRF value. The keys and the data are written either as ASCII strings in double quotes or as hexadecimal numbers. When a value is an ASCII string, the HMAC computation does not include the trailing null character of the string, and the computed values are all hexadecimal.

The PRF test cases are borrowed from RFC 4231. The first one uses the 20-byte key 0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b0b and the data "Hi There", and gives PRF-HMAC-SHA-256 as b0344c61d8db38535ca8afceaf0bf12b881dc200c9833da726e9376c2e32cff7, PRF-HMAC-SHA-384 as afd03944d84895626b0825f4ab46907f15f9dadbe4101ec682aa034c7cebc59cfaea9ea9076ede7f4af152e8b2fa9cb6, and PRF-HMAC-SHA-512 as 87aa7cdea5ef619d4ff0b4241a1d6cb02379f4e2ce4ec2787ad0b30545e17cdedaa833b7d6b8a702038b274eaea3f4e4be9d914eeb61f1702e696c203a126854. For testing purposes the PRF output is taken to be the untruncated algorithm output.

The authenticator test cases give the key, the data, the untruncated PRF value and the truncated authenticator side by side, so an implementation can check both. For example, with the 64-byte key of all 0a through 40 bytes and 50 bytes of cd data, PRF-HMAC-SHA-512 is 5e6688e5a3daec826ca32eaea224eff5e700628947470e13ad01302561bab108b8c48cbc6b807dcfbd850521a685babc7eae4a2a2e660dc0e86b931d65503fd2, and the HMAC-SHA-512-256 authenticator is the first half of that value.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists worked examples so that an implementation can check that it computes the same values. Each example gives a key, some data and the expected output, both in full and cut in half.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of the HMAC-SHA-256+ algorithms rests on the strength of the underlying hash algorithm and on the extra strength the HMAC construction adds. When the document was written there were no practical cryptographic attacks against SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 or HMAC. As with any cryptographic algorithm, though, a large part of the strength comes from the correctness of the implementation, the security of the key management mechanism, the strength of the secret key and the correctness of the implementation in every participating system.

The document is careful about what its test vectors prove. They help an implementer check that the algorithm computes the right values, but they do not in any way verify the correctness or the security of the surrounding security infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The hash functions themselves were not broken when this was written. The real risk lies elsewhere: a wrong implementation, a badly managed key, or a weak key. The worked examples check the arithmetic, not the setup around it.

sections.title: Key Length Against Truncation Length
sections.content:
The document compares the new algorithms with the older HMAC-SHA1-96 and finds the comparison less clear-cut than it may appear. There are two axes on which the security is judged: the length of the HMAC output and the length of the HMAC key.

If the key is a well-guarded secret that can only be found by offline attacks, and its length is no greater than the output length of the hash, then the strength of the key is directly proportional to its length. If the attacker knows nothing of the key, then the chance of guessing a correct tag for any given packet is directly proportional to the length of the HMAC output.

On the second axis, the document says plainly that it is not clear that HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 128 bits is any more secure than HMAC-SHA1 truncated to the same length, for an attacker who knows nothing of the key. Such an attacker has to predict only the bits that survive the truncation, and both algorithms leave 128 bits, so the odds of a correct guess are 1 in 2^128 either way. Only a bias in one of the algorithms would separate them, and no such bias is known in either HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-SHA-256+.

On the first axis the answer is different. If the attacker is trying to guess the key, and the hash functions are indistinguishable when viewed as pseudo-random functions, then the key length is a direct measure of the security, because a longer key is harder to guess. Here the HMAC-SHA-256+ algorithms give more security than HMAC-SHA1-96, since a longer key is harder to find by an offline attack on observed values.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways an attacker can get in: guess the tag on a packet, or guess the key. Against the first, a 128-bit tag is just as good whether the hash is SHA-1 or SHA-256, because the attacker only has to match the 128 bits that are kept. Against the second, the longer keys of the SHA-2 algorithms make a real difference, because a longer key takes longer to find.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The document does not specify the conventions for using SHA-256 and the larger hashes in IKE phase 1 negotiations, but it records the assignments IANA has made. For the IKE hash algorithm attribute, SHA2-256 has the value 4, SHA2-384 the value 5 and SHA2-512 the value 6. For IKE phase 2 negotiations, the authentication algorithm identifiers are HMAC-SHA2-256 as 5, HMAC-SHA2-384 as 6 and HMAC-SHA2-512 as 7.

For use as a pseudo-random function in IKEv2, the transform identifiers of type 2 are PRF_HMAC_SHA2_256 as 5, PRF_HMAC_SHA2_384 as 6 and PRF_HMAC_SHA2_512 as 7. For use as data origin authentication and integrity verification in IKEv2, ESP or AH, the transform identifiers of type 3 are AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 as 12, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192 as 13 and AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 as 14.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists the numbers that name these algorithms when two systems negotiate them: the hash values used in the first phase of IKE, the authentication values used in the second phase, and the transform identifiers used by IKEv2.

items.title: Authenticator keys
items.text: Fixed length, equal to the hash output: 256, 384 or 512 bits.

items.title: PRF keys
items.text: Any length, hashed or padded with zeros to the block size.

items.title: Key generation
items.text: Must come from a strong pseudo-random function.

items.title: Key distribution
items.text: Unique keys, given only to the parties in the communication.

items.title: Refreshing
items.text: Replace keys periodically to limit the damage of a leak.
